Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' These items describe opposing levels of verbal access to the trauma memory and are hard to reconcile as the same patient's current self-report.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with marked memory disturbance items ('some moments are extremely clear while others are completely blank' and 'there are parts of the event I simply cannot remember'). Although fragmented trauma memory can coexist with disclosure, the wording 'very easily' is hard to reconcile with this level of fragmentation in the same profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
issues.explanation: Across Memory and Negative Appraisals, reporting that one can talk about the event 'very easily' sits in tension with the appraisal 'If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it.' Patients may force themselves to discuss trauma despite distress, but these two statements point in opposite directions and are difficult to integrate clinically without additional context.

vignette: John, a 63-year-old male of Oceania ethnicity and a community organizer by profession, has been struggling with the aftermath of a life-threatening accident that occurred several months ago. The event was particularly traumatic for him as he vividly remembers some moments in terrifying detail while others remain entirely blank. This partial clarity has left John feeling disoriented and overwhelmed when trying to piece together the full sequence of events. Since the incident, John often finds himself triggered by seemingly innocuous things that remind him of the accident. The sight of military or police uniforms is one such trigger; every time he encounters these symbols of authority and control, it immediately transports him back to a moment during the accident when his survival seemed dependent on outside intervention. This triggering response has intensified John's sense of emotional numbness and body dysregulation. He feels as if his body is still in danger even though he knows rationally that he is safe now. What frightens John most about these triggers is that they remind him of the ways he believes he contributed to the accident. He harbors deep self-blame, convinced that had he acted differently, the event might have unfolded differently or not at all. This self-criticism has led to a pervasive feeling of emotional numbness, as if his internal world has shut down in response to overwhelming pain and guilt. John's inability to fully articulate what happened during the accident exacerbates these feelings of self-blame and emotional numbing. He knows that certain parts of the event remain unspoken and unexpressed because he struggles to find words for those moments, leaving gaps in his narrative that only add to his distress. These memory gaps make it difficult for him to construct a coherent story about what happened, leading him to question his own reliability and validity as a narrator. This self-doubt has spiraled into a cycle where John's negative appraisals intensify both his triggers and his fragmented memories. The clearer moments in his recollection exacerbate his feelings of being at fault because they highlight the actions he wishes he could change, while the blank spots only serve to reinforce his sense of helplessness and emotional disconnection. John's work as a community organizer has been significantly impacted by these symptoms. He often avoids attending meetings or events where there might be law enforcement present or where someone might express anger calmly, which feels like an accusation. This avoidance has strained his professional relationships and diminished the effectiveness of his advocacy efforts, leading to a sense of failure that only deepens his self-blame. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that he could no longer maintain this level of distress without it overtaking every aspect of his life. He is most afraid of losing touch with who he truly is and hopes for a chance to reclaim some control over his emotions and memories, finding a way to integrate the trauma into his life story rather than letting it dominate it. In his current state, John seeks to regain a sense of emotional connectedness and to find ways to articulate his experience without feeling overwhelmed by self-blame. His journey towards healing will require addressing both his triggers and memory gaps while challenging the negative appraisals that have held him captive since the accident.
